claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite with discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
Untreated W–Cu composites are prone to phase separation under thermal and irradiation stresses.
Untreated W–Cu composites are prone to W–Cu interfacial void formation under thermal and irradiation stresses.
A thin, conformal tungsten carbide or tungsten nitride coating can be deposited on W surfaces by vapor deposition during composite fabrication.
The proposed tungsten carbide or nitride interfacial coating is irradiation-stable.
Plasma-facing fusion components experience severe heat flux, particle exposure, and irradiation.
The cited harsh fusion conditions are directly representative of W–Cu joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components.
The coating forms a robust, conformal barrier at the W–Cu interface.
The coating enhances W–Cu interfacial bonding.
The coating acts as a diffusion barrier at the W–Cu interface.
Increased interfacial adhesion suppresses phase separation and void nucleation under thermal and irradiation loads.
Reduced atomic diffusion across the W–Cu interface suppresses phase separation and void nucleation under thermal and irradiation loads.
Interfacial phase separation and void formation cause thermal-conductivity degradation in untreated W–Cu composites.
Coated W–Cu composites will exhibit less phase separation and interfacial void formation than untreated controls under identical heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Coated W–Cu composites will maintain or improve thermal conductivity relative to untreated controls during service.
The coating approach is applicable to vapor-deposition-processed W–Cu composites used in high-heat-flux, high-irradiation environments.
